steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey paper on recent named entity recognition and relation classification methods, with a focus on few-shot learning. It should define both tasks, explain why the survey covers machine learning and few-shot approaches, position it against earlier surveys, and outline the sections.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- NER and RC: what they are for
- The NER task: formal definition, discontinuous and nested entities
- The RC task: formal definition, link to relation extraction, Figure 1 example
- Scope of the survey: machine learning models only, few-shot focus
- Comparison with existing surveys
- Organization of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- NER and RC: what they are for
  - steps for extracting info from unstructured text into machine-readable format
  - used separately or together in NLP apps: information retrieval, knowledge graph construction/completion, question answering, domain-specific e.g. biomedical data mining (cite)
- The NER task
  - label subsets of words that designate entities; an entity may be several words
  - formal: sequence W of size n, W=\{w_{1},w_{2}...w_{n}\}; learn f(W)=E, E = set of one or more entities, e\subset W
  - discontinuous entity: words not adjacent; "The teams of France and Italy" -> "The team of France", "The team of Italy"
  - nested entities: "The governor of Bryxton" contains sub entity "Bryxton"
  - also classify each entity into predefined types: Person, Location, Organization, etc.
- The RC task
  - does a relation exist between two given entities; classify into predefined semantic relations
  - formal definition (equation); W = \{w_{1},\ w_{2}\...\ w_{n}\}; E=\{(e_{1},e_{2})_{1}..(e_{1},e_{2})_{k}\}
  - pair = subject + object entity, tuple (e_{1},e_{2}); R = relations found for E
  - directed: e_{1} head/subject, e_{2} tail/object; \emptyset = no relation; P = predefined relations
  - Relation Extraction (RE) = NER + RC
  - Figure 1: (a) entities tagged with types (first upper case letter); (b) relations for entity pairs; "Born_in" for "Charles Dickens" / "England"
- Scope
  - survey of recent NER/RC approaches, few-shot focus
  - early methods rule-based / non-ML: text pattern mining (cite), feature-based (cite), graphical (cite); then neural text representations
  - ML-only because: pattern/feature-based score much lower than deep learning on benchmarks per several surveys (cite); few recent models use them alone; non-ML already covered by surveys
  - supervised: astonishing results but lower accuracy with no labels / few labels
  - first handled by weak/distant supervision (cite); noisy labels a problem
  - few-shot learning: branch of meta-learning, few labelled data, small support set (cite); remarkable on NER, RC; adapts to domains, unseen labels -> closer to real world
  - selection methodology -> Section 3
- Existing surveys
  - mostly deep learning; few cover NER + RC together; ours first on both with few-shot focus
  - two surveys: NER only, early approaches + deep learning (cite)
  - one survey: NER and RE, deep learning (cite)
  - one survey: RE, categorized by approach, paths to explore (cite)
- Organization
  - Sec 2 datasets; Sec 3 selection methodology; Sec 4 joint NER+RC models; 5 NER only; Sec 6 RC only; Sec 7 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Relation Classification (RC) are two important steps for extracting information from unstructured text and putting it into a format that machines can read. Many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications use these two steps, sometimes separately and sometimes at the same time. Examples are information retrieval, knowledge graph construction and completion, question answering, and other applications that are specific to a domain, like biomedical data mining.

In the NER task the goal is to label the subsets of words in a text that designate entities. An entity can have more than one word. Formally, if we have a sequence of words W of size n, W=\{w_{1},w_{2}...w_{n}\}, where w is a word in the sequence, then entity tagging means learning the function f(W)=E, where E is a set of one or more e entities and e\subset W. So an entity e can contain multiple w words. The words of an entity do not have to be next to each other, and this kind of entity is called a discontinuous entity. For example the term “The teams of France and Italy" has two entities, “The team of France" and “The team of Italy". Also an entity with multiple words can have sub entities inside it. For example “The governor of Bryxton" is an entity and “Bryxton" is a sub entity, and this kind is called nested entities. NER does not only tag the entities in the text, it also classifies each one into a type from a predefined set of entity types, for example Person, Location, Organization, etc.

The RC task is about identifying whether a relation exists between two given entities, and classifying that relation into one of the predefined semantic relations given in the input. Formally the RC task is defined as:

where W is a sequence of words \{w_{1},\ w_{2}\...\ w_{n}\} and E is a set of one or more entity pairs, E=\{(e_{1},e_{2})_{1}..(e_{1},e_{2})_{k}\}. Each entity pair has a subject entity and an object entity, where an entity e is a sub-sequence of W, so the pair can be written as a tuple (e_{1},e_{2}). R is the set of one or more relations found for E. If the relations are directed, e_{1} is the head or subject entity and e_{2} is the tail or object entity. \emptyset means that there is no relation in any entities pair. P is the set of predefined semantic relations. In the literature, the task that includes both NER and RC is known as Relation Extraction (RE). Figure 1 shows an example where the two tasks are used to extract entities and relations from a sentence. In step (a) the entities are tagged together with their types in the first upper case letter. In step (b) the relations are identified for the entities pairs. For example “ Born_in ” was found as a valid relation for the subject entity “Charles Dickens” and the object entity “England”.

- Scope
  - survey of recent NER/RC approaches, few-shot focus
  - early methods rule-based / non-ML: text pattern mining (cite), feature-based (cite), graphical (cite); then neural text representations
  - ML-only because: pattern/feature-based score much lower than deep learning on benchmarks per several surveys (cite); few recent models use them alone; non-ML already covered by surveys
  - supervised: astonishing results but lower accuracy with no labels / few labels
  - first handled by weak/distant supervision (cite); noisy labels a problem
  - few-shot learning: branch of meta-learning, few labelled data, small support set (cite); remarkable on NER, RC; adapts to domains, unseen labels -> closer to real world
  - selection methodology -> Section 3
- Existing surveys
  - mostly deep learning; few cover NER + RC together; ours first on both with few-shot focus
  - two surveys: NER only, early approaches + deep learning (cite)
  - one survey: NER and RE, deep learning (cite)
  - one survey: RE, categorized by approach, paths to explore (cite)
- Organization
  - Sec 2 datasets; Sec 3 selection methodology; Sec 4 joint NER+RC models; 5 NER only; Sec 6 RC only; Sec 7 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Relation Classification (RC) are two important steps for extracting information from unstructured text and putting it into a format that machines can read. Many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications use these two steps, sometimes separately and sometimes at the same time. Examples are information retrieval, knowledge graph construction and completion, question answering, and other applications that are specific to a domain, like biomedical data mining.

In the NER task the goal is to label the subsets of words in a text that designate entities. An entity can have more than one word. Formally, if we have a sequence of words W of size n, W=\{w_{1},w_{2}...w_{n}\}, where w is a word in the sequence, then entity tagging means learning the function f(W)=E, where E is a set of one or more e entities and e\subset W. So an entity e can contain multiple w words. The words of an entity do not have to be next to each other, and this kind of entity is called a discontinuous entity. For example the term “The teams of France and Italy" has two entities, “The team of France" and “The team of Italy". Also an entity with multiple words can have sub entities inside it. For example “The governor of Bryxton" is an entity and “Bryxton" is a sub entity, and this kind is called nested entities. NER does not only tag the entities in the text, it also classifies each one into a type from a predefined set of entity types, for example Person, Location, Organization, etc.

The RC task is about identifying whether a relation exists between two given entities, and classifying that relation into one of the predefined semantic relations given in the input. Formally the RC task is defined as:

where W is a sequence of words \{w_{1},\ w_{2}\...\ w_{n}\} and E is a set of one or more entity pairs, E=\{(e_{1},e_{2})_{1}..(e_{1},e_{2})_{k}\}. Each entity pair has a subject entity and an object entity, where an entity e is a sub-sequence of W, so the pair can be written as a tuple (e_{1},e_{2}). R is the set of one or more relations found for E. If the relations are directed, e_{1} is the head or subject entity and e_{2} is the tail or object entity. \emptyset means that there is no relation in any entities pair. P is the set of predefined semantic relations. In the literature, the task that includes both NER and RC is known as Relation Extraction (RE). Figure 1 shows an example where the two tasks are used to extract entities and relations from a sentence. In step (a) the entities are tagged together with their types in the first upper case letter. In step (b) the relations are identified for the entities pairs. For example “ Born_in ” was found as a valid relation for the subject entity “Charles Dickens” and the object entity “England”.

In this work we survey recent approaches for the NER and RC tasks, focusing on few-shot learning approaches. The early methods in both tasks used rule-based algorithms, meaning non-machine learning methods, like text pattern mining, feature-based methods or graphical methods. After that came models that used text representation in neural networks. In this survey we only look at machine learning-based models, for a few reasons. First, pattern-based or feature-based models get much lower scores on several benchmarks than deep learning models, according to several surveys. Also, because of these lower scores, only a few models used pattern-based or feature-based methods alone in the last few years. And several surveys have already covered non-machine learning models well enough.

Supervised learning models have got astonishing results in NER and RC, but they have lower accuracy in some practical scenarios, namely when the data has no labels or only a few samples are labelled. At first this problem was handled with weak or distant supervision models. But noisy labels were always an obstacle for getting good results with weak or distant supervision. So a new learning approach was needed to deal with these obstacles. Few-shot learning is a branch of meta-learning that trains on few labelled data and uses a small support set to make predictions. Few-shot learning has shown remarkable performance in several NLP tasks, including NER and RC. Few-shot learning models can also adapt easily to different domains with satisfactory results, because they can use a few samples and handle labels that were not seen during training. For these reasons this discipline is closer to real-world scenarios. So in this survey we select few-shot learning methods as well as supervised learning models. Our methodology for selecting works is shown in Section 3.

Recent surveys focused on deep learning models, and only a few of them surveyed both NER and RC approaches in one study. Our work is the first one that covers the two tasks with a focus on few-shot learning methods. Two of these surveys considered only NER methods, showing the early approaches and focusing on deep learning models. Another survey considered works from NER and RE, also with a focus on deep learning models. And another survey reviewed the works in RE, categorized them by their approaches and then discussed more paths to explore in RE.

The rest of the survey is divided as follows. Section 2 describes the datasets we found to be commonly used in both NER and RC. Section 3 explains how we selected the models for this survey. Section 4 shows models that handle both NER and RC. Section 5 shows the models that only address NER. Section 6 shows the models that only address relation classification. Finally we give our conclusions in Section 7.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Relation Classification (RC) are important steps in extracting information from unstructured text and turning it into a machine-readable format. Several Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications use the two steps, either separately or together, such as information retrieval, knowledge graph construction and completion, question answering and other domain-specific applications, such as biomedical data mining [1].

The NER task aims at labelling subsets of words in text that designate entities. An entity may contain multiple words. Formally, for a sequence of words W of size n, W=\{w_{1},w_{2}...w_{n}\}, where w is a word in the sequence, entity tagging targets learning the function f(W)=E, where E is a set of one or more e entities; e\subset W. An entity e may contain multiple w words. The words within an entity do not need to be adjacent; this type of entity is called a discontinuous entity. For example, the term “The teams of France and Italy" contains two entities “The team of France" and “The team of Italy". An entity of multiple words may also contain sub entities. For example, “The governor of Bryxton" is an entity, and “Bryxton" is a sub entity; this type of entities is called nested entities. The NER task does not only tag entities in text but also classifies each one into a type from a predefined set of entity types, such as Person, Location, Organization, etc.

The RC task aims to identify whether a relation exists between two given entities and to classify the relation into one of the predefined semantic relations given in the input. Formally the RC task is defined as:

where W is a sequence of words \{w_{1},\ w_{2}\...\ w_{n}\}, E is a set of one or more entity pairs; E=\{(e_{1},e_{2})_{1}..(e_{1},e_{2})_{k}\}. Each entity pair consists of a subject entity and an object entity, where an entity e is a sub-sequence of W, so the entity pair can be defined as a tuple (e_{1},e_{2}). R is a set of one or more relations found for E. If the relations are directed, then e_{1} would be a head or subject entity and e_{2} would be a tail or object entity. \emptyset indicates that no relation exists in any entities pair. P is a set of predefined semantic relations. Relation Extraction (RE) is known in the literature as the task that incorporates both the NER and RC tasks. Figure 1 shows an example of using the two tasks to extract entities and relations from a sentence. At step (a), the entities are tagged along with their types in the first upper case letter. At step (b), the relations are identified for entities pairs. For instance, “ Born_in ” was found to be a valid relation for the subject entity “Charles Dickens” and the object entity “England”.

In this work we present a survey on recent approaches in the NER and RC tasks with a focus on few-shot learning approaches. Early methods in both tasks used rule-based algorithms, i.e., non-machine learning methods, such as text pattern mining [2], feature-based methods [3] or graphical methods [4]. These were followed by models that used text representation in neural networks. In this survey, we only consider machine learning-based models for the following reasons: pattern-based or feature-based models have much lower scores on several benchmarks than deep learning models according to several surveys [5,6]. In addition, because of the lower scores, only a few models adopted pattern-based or feature-based methods alone during the last few years. Furthermore, several surveys have already addressed non-machine learning models sufficiently.

Although supervised learning models have achieved astonishing results in the NER and RC tasks, they suffer from lower accuracy in some practical scenarios, namely when data has no labels or only a few samples are labelled. Initially, this issue was handled by weak or distant supervision models [7]. However, noisy labels have always been an obstacle to reaching good results in weak or distant supervision models. Thus, a new learning approach was needed that could tackle these obstacles. Few-shot learning is a branch of meta-learning that conducts training on few labelled data and uses a small support set to perform predictions [8]. Few-shot learning has shown remarkable performance in several NLP tasks including NER and RC. Furthermore, few-shot learning models can easily adapt to various domains with satisfactory results due to their ability to use a few samples and handle labels that were not seen during training. These reasons make this discipline closer to real-world scenarios. Thus, we focus our selection of models in this survey on few-shot learning methods in addition to supervised learning models. Our methodology for selecting works for this survey is described in Section 3.

Recent surveys focused on deep learning models, and only a few considered surveying both NER and RC approaches in a single study. Our work is the first to consider the two tasks with a focus on few-shot learning methods. The surveys in [6,9] considered NER methods only; they showed early approaches and focused on deep learning models. The survey in [5] considered works from the NER and RE tasks, also with a focus on deep learning models. The survey in [10] reviewed the works in the RE task, categorized them based on their approaches, and then discussed further paths in the RE task to be explored.

Our survey is organized as follows: Section 2 describes the datasets that we found commonly used in both the NER and RC tasks. Section 3 explains our methodology for selecting the models for this survey. Section 4 shows the models that handle both the NER and RC tasks. Section 5 shows the models that address the NER task only. Section 6 shows the models that address the relation classification task only. Finally, we conclude with our observations in Section 7.

References:
[1] Quirk and Poon (2016) Chris Quirk and Hoifung Poon. 2016. Distant supervision for relation extraction beyond the sentence boundary. arXiv preprint arXiv:1609.04873 (2016).
[2] Huffman (1995) Scott B Huffman. 1995. Learning information extraction patterns from examples. In International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence . Springer, 246–260.
[3] Kambhatla (2004) Nanda Kambhatla. 2004. Combining lexical, syntactic, and semantic features with maximum entropy models for information extraction. In Proceedings of the ACL interactive poster and demonstration sessions . 178–181.
[4] McClosky et al . (2011) David McClosky, Mihai Surdeanu, and Christopher D Manning. 2011. Event extraction as dependency parsing. In Proceedings of the 49th annual meeting of the association for computational linguistics: human language technologies . 1626–1635.
